Q: Can a php-website 'call' a php file to run on its own (without holding up the website)? A:

If a website-visitor fails at logging in (mistake in username/password), the IP-address will be stored and the visitor has 5 minutes to log in successfully or the IP-address is appended to blocked.txt.

At first it sounds a bit silly. The plan doesn't seem to consider that the user might have been distracted with other tasks (which indeed may be why they failed to log in the first time), and doesn't consider that the same IP address is increasingly often shared by multiple people – not even counting a whole household (or a whole company, or a whole dorm) sharing an IP address, nowadays several different customers might share an IP address.

It could still be useful, but such blocks really need to expire reasonably soon – and I mean in minutes, not hours nor weeks. It's somewhat common to add e.g. a 30 minute lockout after several bad attempts.

I'm struggling with the 5 minute thing, because no matter how I approach this, the entire website is held hostage for the 5 minutes.

Your plan with timers in a separate process can be made to work, but is probably the most complex approach to implement. Each such "timer" process will waste resources all on its own – the 5 minutes are more than enough for someone to attempt 50000 bad logins, which could lead to 50000 php timer processes sitting there consuming your server's RAM (and probably also CPU depending on how they were written).

It's easier to record the time in a database, similar to what RedGrittyBrick suggests in comments, although SQLite might be a better choice than a plain text file (which will eventually grow large enough that scanning it – or removing an entry – can in itself become slow).

I've read about and tried exec("php /home/user/domains/domain.com/public_html/zone/absolve.php > /dev/null &"); This might not be working due to file-rights. I set both php-files to chmod 777, to no avail.

This looks like it would work, as the & together with >/dev/null should cause the exec() function to return immediately. But:

  1. a PHP script called from CLI will not have the visitor's IP address in $_SERVER[] (because it indeed was not called by a web request – the direct relationship is lost), so the address needs to be passed through command-line parameters, or perhaps through setenv();

  2. from the path, it seems like you might be doing this on a "web hosting" account, where it is often disallowed to run external processes, or it could be that any "stray" processes get killed after a short timer;

  3. PHP-in-webserver and PHP-in-CLI are technically two separate packages, so just because you have PHP-in-webserver installed does not imply that you also have php available in CLI, or it might not be in the webserver's $PATH;

  4. as mentioned before, this runs the risk of someone making 50000 bad attempts (not unlikely for a bot) and spawning 50000 processes, so you now also need a lock for each IP address – e.g. a lockfile handled via the flock() function that guarantees only one process can take it.

    and since you're going to keep track of processes, you could much easier keep track of 'start' timestamps directly.

I also tried curl

That won't work, because curl_exec() will of course wait until it receives the whole response – and that only happens when the called PHP script finishes.

Also, your web server has a fixed maximum number of requests it'll handle at a time (and if you're using php-fpm it has its own maximum number of workers), so every such "long-lived" request takes away from being able to serve actual visitors.

Q: Java Spark mapPartitions retry causing duplicate inserts into BigQuery on task failure A:

Spark guarantees at-least-once execution, not exactly-once, when performing external writes inside a transformation like mapPartitions.

When a Spark task fails (due to a network timeout, OOM, or preempted executor), Spark retries the task on another executor. If your mapPartitions code already sent some rows to BigQuery before the failure, the retry will send those same rows again, creating duplicates.

Could use the Official BigQuery Connector instead of mapPartitions for direct inserts. The Spark-BigQuery Connector handles this by writing data to an intermediate GCS location and then using a BigQuery Load Job. Load jobs are atomic; if the Spark job fails, the load never happens, and retries don't result in duplicates.

df.write.format("bigquery").save("dataset.table")

Q: Is it possible to disable updates in PWA? A:

iOS Safari in particular will remove the cache & SW very regularly. It cannot be relied upon to be stable even over the length of a month, much less forever.

If you don't need iOS support, other devices & browsers tend to last longer, but still is a best-effort attempt and comes with no guarantees.

Q: Find out free space on tablespace A:

Better you select from DBA_TABLESPACE_USAGE_METRICS, it shows the REAL size of the tablespace - not a theoretical one.

From the Oracle Database Reference Manual:

If a tablespace has a current size of 5 GB, the combined maximum size of its datafiles is 32 GB, and its underlying storage has 20 GB of free space, then this column will have a value of approximately 25 GB.

SELECT
   m.tablespace_name                                                                    "Tablespace"  ,
   t.status                                                                             "Status"      ,   
   c.files                                                                              "# files"     ,
   to_char(c.bytes /(1024 * 1024 * 1024), '999,999,990.9')                              "Alloc GB"    ,
   to_char(m.used_space * t.block_size /(1024 * 1024 * 1024), '999,999,990.9')          "Used GB"     ,
   to_char(m.tablespace_size * t.block_size /(1024 * 1024 * 1024), '999,999,990.9')     "Max GB"      ,
   to_char(m.used_percent, '90.9')                                                      "% Used"
FROM
   dba_tablespace_usage_metrics m,
   dba_tablespaces              t,
   (select d.name tablespace_name, f.files, f.bytes from sys.ts$ d, (select ts#, count(*) files, sum(bytes) bytes from v$datafile group by ts#) f  where f.ts# = d.ts# 
       union all
    select d.name tablespace_name, f.files, f.bytes from sys.ts$ d, (select ts#, count(*) files, sum(bytes) bytes from v$tempfile group by ts#) f  where f.ts# = d.ts# ) c
WHERE
        m.tablespace_name = t.tablespace_name
    and m.tablespace_name = c.tablespace_name
ORDER BY
   m.tablespace_name ASC ;
